title: Autoscaling, Burst Modes, and Tenancy Controls — Dedicated Capacity PRD (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working PRD for Dedicated Capacity features focused on three linked capabilities: autoscaling patterns, burst capacity modes, and tenancy/isolation controls. The goal is to provide a single source of truth for product, infra, and SRE while we iterate on UX and implementation tradeoffs.

Problem statement:
- Customers buying Dedicated GPU pools need predictable baseline throughput but also occasional headroom for traffic spikes (launches, campaigns, session storms).
- Today Dedicated offers fixed pools + manual capacity changes; customers are asking for: automated scaling with clear cost/latency guarantees, a short-term burst mechanism to absorb spikes, and tenancy knobs to control noisy neighbors and compliance isolation.
- Engineering must avoid complexity explosion: we need simple primitives that map to infra (nodes, pods, allocations) and clear SLAs for fallback behaviors.

Primary goals:
1) Autoscaling that maintains latency SLOs by adjusting active replicas/GPU allocations based on token-per-second load and queueing latency.
2) Burst mode that allows predictable, time-limited overcommit of capacity (short-lived) with configurable limits and cost accounting.
3) Tenancy/isolation controls enabling: per-customer soft isolation (resource reservations + burst caps), strict isolation (dedicated hosts), and workload-class isolation (priority tiers within a tenant).
4) Transparent cost attribution and observability in Redwood Console: token-level cost estimates, burst usage, and rollback events.

Non-goals (for this phase):
- Automatic cross-region failover.
- Continuous model re-compilation or dynamic quantization as part of scaling decisions.
- Auto-rightsizing of GPU types (we’ll support instance family recommendations in a follow-up).

Requirements (user-facing):
- Policy primitives exposed in Console/API:
  - Min capacity (committed GPUs / qps baseline)
  - Max capacity (hard limit to autoscale to)
  - Scale window and cooldown (sec/min)
  - Burst budget (tokens or GPU-seconds per billing period), burst duration cap, and burst priority (high/low)
  - Isolation level: shared, soft-reserved, dedicated-host
- API: Create/update capacity policy via Redwood API (same schema across hosted/dedicated with some dedicated-only fields).
- Notifications: alert when burst consumed > 50%, 90%, and when autoscale hits max cap.
- Billing: burst consumption reported as separate line-item; if burst uses dedicated-hosts, reflect host-hour premium.

Requirements (infra-facing):
- Autoscaler should use a hybrid signal set: token qps, 95p/99p token latency, and queue depth. Prioritize latency SLOs.
- Support warm-standby allocation for fast scale-up (pre-warmed containers or reserved GPU pool that can be attached in <60s).
- Burst implementation options (tradeoffs documented):
  Option A: Soft overcommit by temporarily increasing batch concurrency across runtime processes. Fast but risks per-token latency jitter.
  Option B: Spin up pre-approved host-level capacity (fast if warm-standby, slower if need cold provisioning). Predictable but costs more.
  Option C: Degrade lower-priority customers in same pool (requires per-request priority tagging and fallback models).
- Isolation controls should integrate with tenant network/IAM policies and KMS scoping.

UX / Console flows (early drafts):
- Capacity policy editor: slider for min/max, numeric inputs for burst budget and duration, dropdown for isolation level.
- Visual timeline in Console showing committed baseline, burst events, observed throughput, and costs projected.
- Quickstart template for common patterns: "SG1: steady baseline + monthly marketing burst", "Enterprise: strict dedicated-host + no burst".

APIs (sketch):
- POST /v1/dedicated/policies -> body: {name, min_gpus, max_gpus, scale_window_s, cooldown_s, burst_budget_tokens, burst_duration_s, isolation_level}
- GET /v1/dedicated/policies/{id}/usage -> burst_used, autoscale_events, cost_breakdown
- Events stream: policy_burst_started, policy_burst_ended, autoscale_provisioned, autoscale_failed

SLOs and fallback behavior:
- For soft-shared pools: 99th token latency must remain within committed baseline SLO; if autoscaler cannot provision, fallback to a lighter model variant or degraded responses (configurable).
- For dedicated-host mode: prioritize availability over immediate scale; provide clear time-to-provision expectations in Console.

Monitoring and telemetry:
- New telemetry fields: burst_consumed_gpu_seconds, burst_events_count, autoscale_replicas, time_to_scale_seconds, fallback_trigger_count.
- Dashboards: per-customer capacity timeline, per-route latency impact during bursts, cost per token with burst overlay.

Metrics / success criteria (first 6 months):
- 60% of Dedicated customers adopt autoscale policies for at least one workload.
- During real spikes, 90% of burst events served without >20% latency regression vs baseline.
- Bursts billed separately and average burst revenue uplift for customers who pay = measurable (tracked).

Security & compliance considerations:
- Dedicated-host mode must support FIPS/KMS scoping and audit logs for host attachment/detachment.
- Burst operations should not expose keys or cross-attach customer data to other tenants.

Open questions / tradeoffs to resolve:
- How aggressive should warm standby be? Cost vs speed. Proposal: tiered warm pools (fast warm, cold warm) and let tenant pick.
- Pricing model: per-GPU-hour for baseline + per-GPU-second for burst vs token-based burst metering. Need finance input.
- Enforcement of burst budgets: strict denial vs queued requests vs degraded model.
- Should burst be global across regions or scoped per-region?

Implementation outline & dependencies:
- Infra: autoscaler service enhancements + warm-standby resource pool (Infra owner: Carlos Rivera).
- Runtime: support priority tags and graceful degradation (owner: Applied ML runtime team).
- Console: policy editor + timeline visualization (owner: Console and Rollouts).
- Billing: line-iteming for burst (Finance + Billing infra).

Phased rollout plan (high level):
- M1 (experiments, internal): implement autoscaler signal set, simple min/max policies, enable on internal tenant clusters. Duration: 8 weeks.
- M2 (beta customers): add burst budget plumbing, expose in Console as beta, collect telemetry. Duration: 10 weeks.
- M3 (GA): add dedicated-host tenancy, billing integration, and hardened fallback policies. Duration: 8 weeks.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: noisy neighbor impact during soft bursts. Mitigation: rate-limited burst and per-route priority tagging + circuit breaker.
- Risk: cost surprises for customers. Mitigation: strict budget alerts, simulated cost preview, opt-in for burst by default turned off.
- Risk: long provisioning time for hosts. Mitigation: warm standby and clear Console messaging on TDTP (time-to-fully-provision).

Notes / discussion fragments (working):
- "We should add a \"campaign mode\" preset that gives a high burst budget for up to 3 hours and then forces cooldown. Marketing likes simple presets." — Mei
- "If we expose model fallback rules, we can keep latency tight by trading down models instead of trying to spin up more GPUs mid-request." — Sam
- "Priority queues need an admission-controller change; track as infra epic." — Carlos

Next steps before formal PRD:
- Engineering spike on warm-standby options + cost model (2 weeks).
- Finance to propose burst pricing and billing model (1 week).
- UX mockups for policy editor and timeline (2 weeks).
- Identify 2 anchor customers for beta (customer success).

References and links:
- Linear tickets (see linked_artifacts)
- Prior notes: shared_drives/engineering/serving-runtime/autoscale-signals-notes (internal sketch)

Action items:
- Asha: kick off infra spike and schedule 30-min sync with Carlos + Sam this week.
- Mei: mockups for Console policy editor by 2026-03-17.
- Nadia: reach out to billing to prototype line-iteming.
